Appetite and drinking: eating less, refusing food, drinking much more or much less than usual
Energy and behavior: hiding, restlessness, sleepiness, confusion, clingy behavior, seeming painful, not wanting to move
Breathing: faster than usual, effort to breathe, open-mouth breathing, coughing, wheezing, noisy breathing
Vomiting or diarrhea: how many times, any blood, whether Rowan can keep water down
Urination and stool: straining, accidents, no urine, very frequent urination, black or bloody stool
Walking and balance: limping, wobbling, weakness, trouble standing or jumping
Mouth and gums: pale, blue, gray, very red, dry, sticky, or swollen
Belly and posture: bloated abdomen, repeated stretching, hunched posture, guarding the belly
Pain signs: crying, flinching, panting when resting, licking one spot, not wanting to be touched
Exposure risks: possible toxin, broken bone, bite, fall, heat, or new medicine

This becomes urgent right away if Rowan has any of these:

Trouble breathing, blue or pale gums, collapse, or can’t stand
Seizure, unresponsiveness, or extreme weakness
A swollen or painful belly, especially with retching or repeated unproductive vomiting
Heavy bleeding that won’t stop
Suspected poisoning, chewing human meds, xylitol, chocolate, rodent bait, lilies, or another toxin
Repeated vomiting, repeated diarrhea, or cannot keep water down
No urination, straining to urinate, or a blocked-looking urinary effort
Sudden severe pain, severe limping, or a possible broken bone
A very young, older, or medically fragile pet acting off, even if the signs seem mild

If Rowan is only a little off but still breathing normally, walking, and keeping food and water down, monitor closely for the next several hours and call your vet today if the change lasts, worsens, or you notice any of the signs above.
